title: Wishing well, even on them
told: a story from the Buddhist commentaries

hook.say: yesterday i left you with an open question. today i have a new one. is there someone in your life right now who is just hard to like?
options: they come with the job, don’t they? listen.
that’s the hardest kind. listen gently.
then you’re lucky. keep this one for a bad week.

steps.line: Long ago, a group of monks went deep into a forest to spend the rainy season meditating at the foot of its great trees.
But the tree spirits who lived there didn’t want them. At night they sent frightening shapes, strange sounds and foul smells to drive the monks away.

steps.q: The frightened monks run back to the Buddha. What do you think he tells them?
o: “Go back to that very same forest.”
“Stay here with me until the rains end.”
steps.why: Back to the very same trees, the commentary says. Same forest, same spirits, but this time the monks would bring something with them.

steps.line: Shaking, the monks told the Buddha everything. “Go back to the same forest,” he said. “This time, take protection with you.”
The protection was a teaching on metta, friendliness. Wish every being well, he said, the way a mother guards her only child.

steps.q: Why send them back to the spirits who scared them, instead of somewhere safer?
o: The spirits were never really there
He wanted to test how brave they were
Their fear would follow them anywhere
steps.why: A new forest would have new shadows. Running moves your body; it doesn’t move your fear.

steps.line: The monks walked back chanting it, wishing even the spirits well. The spirits felt it. They softened, and began to watch over the monks instead.

steps.q: The teaching says to love every being the way a mother protects her only child. Why that picture?
o: Because the Buddha’s own mother died young
It’s the most selfless love people know
Because the monks were young, like children
steps.why: A mother would give her life for her only child. The Metta Sutta asks for that same care, stretched without limit to every being, even the ones who scared you.

steps.q: Buddhist teachers warn that metta has a “near enemy”: something that looks like it but isn’t. What is it?
o: Clingy affection that wants something back
Plain dislike you try to hide
Being too shy to say how you feel
steps.why: In the Visuddhimagga, metta’s far enemy is ill will, and its near enemy is selfish attachment, which can pass for love. Metta wishes well and asks nothing back.

steps.line: Today, the coworker who replies all. Metta doesn’t ask you to like them, or to agree. Just: may you be at ease.
steps.label: today

say: metta comes from mitta, a friend. it’s friendliness: the plain, warm wish for someone’s good, pointed at anyone at all. the buddha’s own verses say hatred never ends by hatred, only by its opposite. an old rule, he called it.
theravada monks still chant this teaching for protection, just as the forest monks did. every school knows the same word in maitreya, metteyya in pali: the friendly one, the buddha still to come.

steps.q: The spirits changed only after the monks did. So what does metta work on first?
o: Your own heart first, then others
steps.why: It starts at home. The traditional order of practice even begins with yourself: may i be at ease.

today.say: today, pick one person who is hard to like. three times, on an out-breath, think: may you be at ease. you don’t have to feel warm. just send it.
options: that’s the old way too: start with yourself, then someone easy.

sources: Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sutta Nipata 1.8; Khuddakapatha 9): the mother protecting her only child; a boundless heart toward all beings
Paramatthajotika (commentary on the Sutta Nipata and Khuddakapatha): the origin story of the monks, the forest spirits who frightened them, and the Buddha sending them back with this sutta
Dhammapada 5: hatred does not cease by hatred, but by love; an old rule
Maitreya (Pali Metteyya), the future buddha, named from maitri/metta
check: The commentary gives a number of monks (traditionally five hundred) and a forest near the Himalayas; both are left out here.
The spirits’ reason (they could not stay in their trees above the monks) is left out; the shapes, sounds and smells are paraphrased.
